back: 1 u = 1/12th of the mass of a carbon-12 atom = 1.660539 x 10^-27 kg = 931.5 MeV/c^2. Used because atomic masses in kg are inconveniently small (a carbon atom is 1.99 x 10^-26 kg).
A,Z X: Z = number of protons, N = number of neutrons, A = Z + N = number of nucleons. Example: 197,79 Au has 197 nucleons, 79 protons and 118 neutrons.
Isotopes: same Z, different N (1,1 H and 2,1 H). Isobars: same A (3,1 H and 3,2 He). Isotones: same N, different Z (198,80 Hg and 197,79 Au, both N = 118).
mp = 1.00727 u = 1.67262 x 10^-27 kg; mn = 1.00866 u = 1.6749 x 10^-27 kg. The proton mass equals the hydrogen atom mass (1.00783 u) minus the electron mass (0.00055 u).

Discovered by Chadwick in 1932 (beryllium bombarded with alpha-particles; photons ruled out by energy-momentum conservation). A free neutron decays into a proton, an electron and an antineutrino with a mean life of about 1000 s; bound neutrons are stable.
R = R0 A^(1/3), with R0 = 1.2 fm = 1.2 x 10^-15 m. Established from alpha-particle scattering and, more accurately, from electron scattering.

rho = m / [(4/3) pi R0^3] = about 2.3 x 10^17 kg m^-3, independent of A, because volume grows in proportion to the number of nucleons. Nuclei resemble drops of a constant-density liquid; neutron-star matter is comparably dense.
E = mc^2, with c = 3 x 10^8 m/s. Mass is another form of energy; 1 g of matter is equivalent to 9 x 10^13 J.
1 u = 1.4924 x 10^-10 J = 931.5 MeV/c^2. Worked out by multiplying the mass of 1 u by c^2 and converting joules to MeV.
Delta M = [Z mp + (A - Z) mn] - M, the difference in mass between a nucleus and its separated constituents. Always positive: the bound nucleus is lighter.

Eb = Delta M c^2: the energy released when the nucleons come together, and the energy needed to pull the nucleus apart. Binding energy per nucleon Ebn = Eb/A measures how tightly each nucleon is held.

Ebn rises steeply for light nuclei, is flat at about 8 MeV for 30 < A < 170, peaks at about 8.75 MeV for A = 56, and falls to about 7.6 MeV at A = 238. Energy is released by fission of heavy nuclei and fusion of light ones, both moving towards the peak.

Because the force falls to zero beyond a few femtometres, a nucleon interacts only with its near neighbours. If a nucleon has at most p neighbours, its binding energy is about pk (k an energy constant), so Ebn is roughly constant instead of growing with A.

Much stronger than the Coulomb force (so it can overcome proton-proton repulsion); short range, a few femtometres; charge independent (n-n, p-n and p-p all approximately equal); no simple mathematical form like Coulomb's or Newton's law.
The potential energy of a pair of nucleons is minimum at r0 = 0.8 fm. For r > r0 the force is attractive; for r < r0 it is strongly repulsive.

Becquerel discovered it in 1896. It is a nuclear phenomenon in which an unstable nucleus decays: alpha-decay emits a helium nucleus, beta-decay emits electrons or positrons, gamma-decay emits high-energy photons.

Decay constant lambda: s^-1. Half-life T1/2: time for half the initial nuclei to decay, unit s. Mean life tau: time for the number to fall to e^-1 of its initial value, unit s. Activity R: Bq (s^-1). Only energy is measured in MeV.
Half-life leaves 50% of the nuclei; mean life leaves about 37% (e^-1). So the mean life is the longer of the two, and neither may be written in energy units.
n + 235,92 U -> 236,92 U -> 144,56 Ba + 89,36 Kr + 3n (or Sb + Nb + 4n, or Xe + Sr + 2n). The fragments are radioactive and emit beta-particles in succession.

About 200 MeV per fissioning nucleus. Estimate: an A = 240 nucleus has Ebn = 7.6 MeV, the A = 120 fragments have 8.5 MeV, so 240 x 0.9 = 216 MeV is released. The energy first appears as kinetic energy of fragments and neutrons, then as heat.

Fusion needs the nuclei to approach within a few fm. The barrier is about 400 keV for two protons (higher for larger Z). (3/2)kT = 400 keV gives T about 3 x 10^9 K; fusion driven by such heating is called thermonuclear fusion.
4 1,1 H + 4e^- -> 4,2 He + 2e^- + 2 neutrino + 6 gamma + 26.7 MeV. Four hydrogen nuclei give one helium nucleus, the energy source of the Sun; helium later fuses into carbon at about 10^8 K.
Chemical reactions involve a few eV; nuclear reactions MeV, about a million times more for the same mass. Fission of 1 kg of uranium gives about 10^14 J; burning 1 kg of coal gives about 10^7 J.
